key: (Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.
s: The chapter says that, nameless, the Tao is the Originator of heaven and earth, and named, the Mother of all things; Wang Bi, on chapter 1, reads it as saying that all that exists begins in non-being, and that the Tao, without form or name, first begins all things and then rears them as their mother.
src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 1, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

evidence.words: 凡有皆始於無，故「未形」「無名」之時，則為萬物之始。及其「有形」「有名」之時，則長之、育之、亭之、毒之，為其母也。道以無形無名始成萬物。
evidence.gloss: All that exists begins in non-being; so at the time before form and name it is the beginning of all things, and when form and name come it grows, rears, shapes and matures them, being their mother. The Tao, formless and nameless, begins and completes all things.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref Tao Te Ching 1, at [0]) and Wang Bi comments on exactly this line (無名，天地之始，有名，萬物之母) in his base text. His comment carries every part of the reading: 凡有皆始於無 (all that exists begins in non-being), the nameless stage as beginning and the named stage as the mother that grows and rears things, and 道以無形無名始成萬物. Plain sense avoids leaning on Legge’s parentheses (nameless / named). Source line names the packet edition. Entry passes entry-check.
